question: Does Jesus judge people?
summary: John 5:22, John 5:26-27, John 9:39, Acts 17:31, 2 Corinthians 5:10, and Revelation 19:11 say Jesus judges everyone, with the Father committing all judgment to the Son. John 8:15 and John 12:47 have Jesus himself say "I judge no man" and "I came not to judge the world, but to save the world." The Johannine Jesus both claims and denies the role of judge within the same gospel.

reconcile.connective: Commentators resolve the apparent clash by reading "judge" in two senses — Christ came at first to save, not condemn, holding the forensic role of Judge in reserve for a day still to come.

discrepancy.connective: The sharpest critical reading comes from Rudolf Bultmann, who traced John's futurist judgment sayings to an ecclesiastical redactor overlaying an evangelist whose own theology already located judgment in the present response to Jesus's word.

skeptic.name: Rudolf Bultmann
skeptic.work: The Gospel of John: A Commentary
skeptic.attribution: Rudolf Bultmann, The Gospel of John: A Commentary, trans. G. R. Beasley-Murray et al. (Philadelphia: Westminster Press, 1971; German orig. Das Evangelium des Johannes, 1941)

pd_work.resource: John Haley, An Examination of the Alleged Discrepancies of the Bible (1874)
pd_work.author: John Haley
pd_work.note: Haley treats this exact cluster verbatim under a 'To judge the world. / Not to judge.' parallel-text table (citing John 5:22,27; 8:15; 9:39; 12:47) and resolves it via the two senses of Greek krino (to judge vs. to condemn) plus a present-mission/second-coming distinction: "'I judge no man,' i.e. after your manner, or else, during my present mission. At his second coming 'he will' in the ultimate and highest sense, 'judge the world.'" (p. 120).

link.title: John 3:17—Did Jesus come to judge the world or not?
link.note: Live apologetic treatment citing John 5:22, 5:27, 8:15, 9:39, and 12:47; argues the 'not to judge' sayings concern Christ's first coming/earthly ministry while the 'all judgment committed' sayings concern his second coming.

excerpts.attribution: John Gill, Exposition of the Entire Bible (1746-63)
excerpts.excerpt_text: Christ did not take upon him to judge and determine in civil affairs, or in things pertaining to a court of judicature among men; this was not his province; an instance of this there is in the context, in not condemning the woman brought to him; nor did he judge the persons and states of men, or proceed to pass any sentence of condemnation on them; he came not to condemn, but save the world; this was not his business now; otherwise, all judgment is committed to him, and which he will exercise another day.
excerpts.on_tension_rationale: Gill reconciles v.15's 'I judge no man' with the 'all judgment committed to the Son' texts by restricting the denial to Christ's present civil/forensic role, reserving universal judgment for 'another day.'
excerpts.source_note_text:
Ye judge after the flesh,.... According to their carnal affections and prejudices; taking the Messiah to be a temporal prince, and his kingdom to be of this world, they judged that Jesus could not be he; they looked upon him as a mere man, and seeing him in much outward meanness, in his human nature, they judged of him according to this outward appearance: or "ye" that are "after the flesh judge"; to which sense the Persic version agrees, "for ye are carnal"; and so judged as carnal men, who are very improper persons to judge of spiritual things:
I judge no man; in the same way, after the flesh, or in a carnal manner, nor according to outward appearances, according to the sight of the eyes, or the hearing of the ears: Christ did not take upon him to judge and determine in civil affairs, or in things pertaining to a court of judicature among men; this was not his province; an instance of this there is in the context, in not condemning the woman brought to him; nor did he judge the persons and states of men, or proceed to pass any sentence of condemnation on them; he came not to condemn, but save the world; this was not his business now; otherwise, all judgment is committed to him, and which he will exercise another day.
